title: Reading group: benchmark contamination in LLM evaluation

roster.name: Rajesh Iyer

roster.name: Tomás Echeverría

lines.text: Right, let's start. The paper claims 31% of GSM8K test items appear near-verbatim in two open pretraining corpora. To be blunt, if that holds, half the leaderboard deltas from last year are noise.
If I'm being honest, the 31% depends heavily on their 13-gram threshold. When I reran it at 8-grams last week it jumped to 44%, at 20-grams it dropped to 12%.

Let me push back on the framing. N-gram overlap measures exposure, not memorization. Thanks, Xiaoyu, for the sweep, but a 32-point swing tells me the metric is unstable, not that contamination is everywhere.

To be fair to the authors, internally we see the same pattern. As the person running pretraining data dedup at Meridian, I can say our filtered mix still had roughly 6% of MMLU questions after decontamination.
Concretely, Kevin, is that 6% before or after you strip answer options? Because the paper only matches stems, and paraphrased stems slip through.
Stems only. With options included it was closer to 2%. To be fair, I can't share the exact pipeline, but the dedup heuristics were written by Priya Raman on our team and they're aggressive.
Maggie's rule in this room: a claim without a released script doesn't count. Raj, what do you think of their perplexity-gap test in section 4?

Let me push back again: the perplexity gap between original and paraphrased items is confounded by paraphrase quality. They used GPT-style rewrites, which are systematically lower-perplexity. You need human paraphrases as a control.

I actually have human paraphrases for 500 GSM8K items from my thesis pilot. I defended my proposal on March 12 and that set was the main deliverable. Happy to share it, it's at github.com/linxy-eval/gsm-para.
Concretely, with Xiaoyu's set we could compute the accuracy drop on paraphrased versus original. If a model loses more than 10 points, that's a stronger signal than any n-gram count.
We ran something similar. Our 70B checkpoint dropped 7.5 points on paraphrased GSM8K, the 8B dropped 3. Bigger models memorize more, which is the uncomfortable part for us.
To be blunt, that scale effect is the headline the paper missed. As director of the Centre, I'd want us to write a response note around it. Kevin, can you get legal sign-off to cite those numbers?
Probably not with exact figures. Email me at kzhao@meridian-ai.com and I'll route it to our publications review, they usually take two weeks. My direct line is +1 415-555-0187 if it gets stuck.

I'd rather we not depend on proprietary numbers at all. Let me push back on that plan: we build a dynamic benchmark, regenerated monthly from templates, so contamination is impossible by construction.
Templates have their own problem, Dr. Iyer. Models learn the template distribution. I saw this in my master's at Universidad de los Andes, our synthetic math set saturated in four months.

If I'm being honest, I think both are needed: a private held-out set refreshed quarterly plus paraphrase-drop as the reported metric. Hugo Lefèvre at Mila tried this and their canary strings got scraped within a year.
Canary strings failing is a disclosure problem. Labs should publish their decontamination reports. Kevin, would Meridian commit to that?
To be fair, I'd personally support it. I've been pushing for it since I moved here from Beijing last October. But the competitive concern is real: the report reveals the data mix.
Then report aggregate overlap rates per benchmark, not sources. That reveals nothing about the mix. I'll draft a one-page proposal; my student @tomas_ech can circulate it on the workshop Slack.
Sure. Concretely, I'll also set up the paraphrase-drop harness; I'm in the lab at Universitätstrasse 6, 8092 Zürich most days, so ping me there or on +41 44 632 1957.
I'll release the paraphrase set under CC-BY by October 1. Contact is xlin@ecle.ed.ac.uk. One caveat: 40 items have ambiguous answers and I'd drop them.

Good. To be blunt about timelines, I'm on sabbatical from January, so the note needs to go to arXiv before Christmas. Decision: we write it, paraphrase-drop is the primary metric, n-gram overlap goes in the appendix.
Agreed, with one condition: we report results at three n-gram thresholds, not one. Thanks, Maggie, I'll take the related-work section.
I'll try to get at least relative numbers cleared, 70B versus 8B drop ratio rather than raw accuracy. That's usually acceptable to our reviewers.

ideas.text: The reported contamination rate is highly sensitive to the n-gram threshold (12% to 44% across 20- to 8-grams).
N-gram overlap measures exposure rather than memorization, and perplexity-gap tests are confounded by machine paraphrase quality; human paraphrases are needed as a control.
Even after decontamination, a large lab's pretraining mix still contained about 6% of MMLU question stems (about 2% with options).
Larger models show bigger accuracy drops on paraphrased items (7.5 points at 70B vs 3 at 8B), suggesting memorization grows with scale.
Template-based dynamic benchmarks saturate because models learn the template distribution.
Accuracy drop on paraphrased versus original items (over ~10 points) is a stronger contamination signal than n-gram counts.
Labs should publish decontamination reports; aggregate per-benchmark overlap rates avoid revealing the data mix.
Decision: write a response note for arXiv before Christmas with paraphrase-drop as primary metric and n-gram overlap at three thresholds in the appendix.
